0: This is the first page of the book, and it is not about any one tool. It is about how to learn tools. Everything after this Part teaches a specific technology (JavaScript, HTTP, Git, NestJS, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Kubernetes) using the same small set of questions: why does it exist, what is the mental model, how does it work inside, how does it fail, what does it trade away.
1: Programming Fundamentals in JavaScript and TypeScript

Welcome to Volume 0. This volume exists for one reader: the person who wants to become a backend engineer and is starting close to zero. Maybe you have written a little JavaScript in a browser, maybe you have followed a tutorial once, maybe you have never written a line.
2: Backend code spends most of its life waiting. It waits for the database to answer a query, for a payment provider to respond, for a file to be read from disk, for another service across the network.
3: Before you build a backend, you need a clear picture of what a backend actually does. A backend is a program that sits on a computer somewhere, waits for requests to arrive over the internet, and sends back responses. That is the whole job, at the highest level.
4: Your code runs on Linux. Not on your laptop's friendly desktop, but on a Linux server in a data center, inside a container, reached over a text-only connection. When your backend misbehaves at 2 a.m., you will not click buttons to fix it; you will type commands into a terminal.
5: Git Basics and the Development Workflow

Every real software project uses version control, and in practice that means Git. Git records the history of your code: every change, who made it, when, and why. It lets many people work on the same codebase without overwriting each other, lets you undo mistakes, and lets you see how any line of code came to be.
6: This is the Part where everything in Volume 0 comes together. You know TypeScript (Part 1), asynchronous code (Part 2), how the web works (Part 3), the command line (Part 4), and Git (Part 5).
7: In Part 6 you built a products API: NestJS, PostgreSQL, validated input, one error shape, tests and Docker. You talked to it with curl. Real users do not use curl. They open a browser, see a page, fill in a form and press a button.
10: A data structure is a way of arranging data in memory so that certain operations are cheap. That is the whole idea. An array makes "give me item number 4,096" cheap. A hash map makes "give me the record for key order:8813" cheap. A heap makes "give me the most urgent job" cheap.
11: Most backend engineers meet algorithms twice: once in an interview, and then again at 02:00 when an endpoint that "worked fine in staging" takes 40 seconds in production. This part is about the second meeting.
13: Operating Systems and the Node.js Runtime

A NestJS application is a single operating-system process running one JavaScript thread on top of V8 and libuv. Every production incident you will ever debug in that application eventually bottoms out in one of a handful of operating-system ideas: a process ran out of memory, a file descriptor leaked, a signal was ignored, a thread blocked, a scheduler throttled you, a lock was taken in the wrong order.
14: Every request your NestJS application serves has already survived a long journey before your controller sees it. It was a DNS lookup, then a TCP handshake, then a TLS negotiation, then a stream of bytes parsed into an HTTP request, then a load balancer decision, and only then a JavaScript object called req.
15: Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change later. Which process runs which code, which database owns which table, which team can deploy without asking another team, how a request travels from the load balancer to the row on disk.
16: Clean Code Principles and Design Patterns
Part 15 covered the shape of systems: which process runs what, who owns which data. This part goes one level down, to the shape of code inside a module.
17: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a way of building software where the business problem shapes the code, not the database schema and not the framework. It was described by Eric Evans in 2003, and twenty years later it is still the most useful vocabulary we have for organising a large backend.
18: An API is a contract you will be held to for years. The database schema behind it can change every sprint; the API cannot, because mobile apps stuck on last year's release and partner integrations nobody remembers are calling it right now. That asymmetry is why API design deserves more care than almost any other backend decision.
19: REST (Part 18) is the default API style in this book, and for good reason: it is simple, universal and predictable. But it is not the only style, and a senior engineer chooses the right one for each situation.
20: Most backend developers meet the database as "the place where the ORM puts things". That is like meeting an aircraft engine as "the place where the noise comes from". This part goes underneath.
21: SQL is the one language every backend engineer writes that runs on someone else's execution engine, against data they cannot see, with a cost that scales with a table they do not control. Writing it well means knowing what the planner will do with it.
22: PostgreSQL is the component in your stack that you can least afford to treat as a black box. Redis can be restarted. A NestJS pod can be killed and replaced.
23: Part 22 taught you how PostgreSQL stores and protects your data: pages, buffers, WAL, MVCC, VACUUM, statistics, locks, and the planner. This part is about the one structure you will add, remove, argue about and get paged for more than any other: the index.
24: Every backend bug that costs real money has the same shape: two things happened at the same time and the code assumed they would not. Two customers bought the last unit. Two workers picked up the same job. A payment was recorded but the order was not. A commit was acknowledged and then vanished when the disk lost power.
25: ORM Engineering: TypeORM, Sequelize and Raw SQL
An ORM (object-relational mapper) is a translation layer between the objects your TypeScript code works with and the rows PostgreSQL stores.
26: Most backend systems never outgrow one PostgreSQL instance. That sentence surprises people, so let me put numbers on it. A single well-tuned PostgreSQL server on a modern machine (say 32 vCPU, 128 GB RAM, NVMe storage) handles tens of thousands of simple indexed queries per second, several thousand write transactions per second, and multiple terabytes of data.

Two questions define this part. How do you change a production database without breaking old application versions? And how do you change an API or an event without breaking old clients?
29: This book's default datastore is PostgreSQL, and that is a deliberate, defensible default: a relational database with transactions, constraints, joins and a mature ecosystem is the right choice for most backends most of the time.
30: Most developers meet caching as "put Redis in front of the database and things get faster". That sentence is true and dangerous in equal measure. It is true because a Redis read costs about 0.3 ms and a PostgreSQL query costs 2 to 20 ms.
31: Messaging: Queues, Topics, Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS

Every backend starts synchronous. A request comes in, the handler does everything it needs to do, and a response goes out. That model is simple and it works until the "everything" grows: POST /orders must charge the card, reserve stock, send an email, notify the warehouse, update analytics, and refresh the recommendation model.
32: Imagine two friends, Asha and Ben, who share one notebook of orders for their small bakery. 34: Reliability Engineering: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Backpressure

Every backend system is a chain of things that can break. Your NestJS process talks to PostgreSQL, to Redis, to Kafka, to a payment gateway, to an email provider, and to three other services owned by other teams. Each of those calls crosses a network.
35: "Node is single-threaded, so I don't have to think about race conditions." Every backend engineer has heard this, and most have believed it at some point. It is wrong in a way that costs money: oversold inventory, double payments, duplicated emails, cron jobs that run five times because there are five pods.
36: Every product eventually stores files. Profile pictures, invoices as PDF, product images, KYC documents, CSV imports, chat attachments, voice notes. Most developers meet this the same way: multer writes the upload to ./uploads, a column stores the path, and it works on the laptop.
37: Developers use the word "search" for three things that have almost nothing in common: Relevance is the thing that separates search from filtering. Relevance is a score that estimates how well a document answers a query, so the results can be ordered by that score. Filtering has no score. Lookup has no ordering.
38: Real-Time Systems: WebSockets, SSE and Pub/Sub

HTTP was built for a client that asks and a server that answers. Real-time features invert that: the server has something to say and the client is waiting. A driver moved 200 metres, a payment was captured, a colleague typed a character.
39: There is a moment in every backend engineer's career when a POST /orders endpoint that used to answer in 90 ms starts answering in 6 seconds, and nobody changed the order logic.

44: Security is the one area of backend engineering where a single missing if statement is a headline. A slow query costs you latency. A missing index costs you money. A missing ownership check on GET /orders/:id costs you every customer's address, and possibly the company.

1.1: A value is a piece of data your program works with. The number 4200, the text "pending", the fact true — each is a value. JavaScript has a small set of built-in kinds of value called primitive types. You will use these constantly.

1.1.2: Variables: let, const and the ghost of var

A variable is a named bin that holds a value. In modern JavaScript you declare variables with const or let. const means the bin's contents will not be reassigned. let means they might be. There is an older keyword, var, which you should never use in new code; we explain why so you recognize it in old code.
1.1.3: JavaScript has two equality operators. === (strict equality) compares value and type with no conversion. == (loose equality) converts the operands to a common type first, with rules so surprising that professionals simply never use it. "Truthiness" is the set of rules for which values count as true in an if.
1.2: TypeScript types: the second half of the language

TypeScript lets you write down what type a variable, parameter or return value is supposed to be, and then a compiler checks that you never violate it. The types are erased before the code runs — Node never sees them — so types cost nothing at runtime. Their entire value is catching mistakes before the code ever runs.

1.4.2: Scope, closures and the call stack

Scope is the set of variables a piece of code can see. A closure is a function that remembers the variables from where it was created, even after that place has finished running. The call stack is the list of functions currently in progress. These three ideas explain a lot of otherwise-mysterious behavior.

1.5.2: Arrays and the methods you will actually use
An array is an ordered list of values. An order has a list of items; a page of results is a list of orders; a user has a list of addresses. Arrays hold those lists.
1.5.3: Maps, Sets and when to use them

A Map is a collection of key-value pairs where keys can be any type (not just strings). A Set is a collection of unique values. They complement objects and arrays: use a Map for a lookup table, a Set for "have I seen this before?".

1.8.2: this, and how it is bound

Inside a method, this means "the object this method was called on". The catch is the word called: this is decided at the moment of the call, by how the call is written, not by where the method was defined. Call cart.totalCents() and this is cart. Take the method out of the object and call it on its own, and this is undefined.

1.8.5: Both describe a contract that other classes fulfil. An interface is a pure shape: names and types, no code, erased at runtime. 10.1: Why a backend engineer must care about data structures

A data structure is a way of arranging data in memory so that certain operations are cheap. That is the whole idea. An array makes "give me item number 4,096" cheap. A hash map makes "give me the record for key order:8813" cheap. A heap makes "give me the most urgent job" cheap.
10.10: A tree is a set of nodes connected parent-to-child with exactly one path between any two nodes. One node is the root; nodes without children are leaves; the number of edges from the root to a node is its depth; the longest such path is the tree's height.
10.12: A heap is a binary tree with two rules: it is complete (every level is full except possibly the last, which fills left to right), and it obeys the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is smaller than or equal to its children, so the smallest item is always at the root. A max-heap flips the comparison.
10.13: A priority queue is an abstract type: insert items with a priority, and always remove the item with the highest priority (or the earliest deadline, or the lowest cost).
10.14: A trie (pronounced "try", from re*trie*val) is a tree where each edge carries one character and each path from the root spells a prefix. Every key that shares a prefix shares the nodes for that prefix. A node is marked terminal when the path to it spells a complete key.
10.15: A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) connected by edges. Edges may be directed (A follows B does not mean B follows A) or undirected (A and B are friends), weighted (the road from A to B takes 7 minutes) or unweighted. A graph with no directed cycles is a DAG (directed acyclic graph), the shape of every dependency system.
10.16: A Bloom filter is a set that can be wrong in exactly one direction. Ask it "is X in the set?" and it answers either "definitely not" or "probably yes".
10.17: An LRU (least recently used) cache is a bounded key-value store that, when full, evicts the entry that has gone longest without being read or written.
10.4: A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node (a singly linked list), or pointers to both the next and the previous node (a doubly linked list). Nodes are allocated one at a time anywhere in memory; nothing is contiguous.
10.5: A stack is a collection where you add and remove from the same end: last in, first out (LIFO). The operations are push (add on top), pop (remove the top) and peek (look at the top).
10.6: A queue is first in, first out (FIFO): you add at the back (enqueue) and remove from the front (dequeue). It is the data structure of waiting. Every job system, message broker, request buffer and event loop is a queue with extra guarantees layered on top.
10.7: A deque (double-ended queue, pronounced "deck") supports O(1) insertion and removal at both ends: pushFront, pushBack, popFront, popBack. A queue is a deque you only use one way; a stack is a deque you only use at one end.
10.8: A hash map (hash table, dictionary) stores key-value pairs and finds a value by its key in O(1) on average. It does this by running the key through a hash function that produces a number, using that number to pick a bucket in an array, and storing the pair there.
10.9: A set stores unique values and answers "is X in here?" in O(1) on average. JavaScript's Set is the same ordered hash table as Map without the value slot.
11.1: Big O — what it measures and what it hides

Big O notation describes how the cost of an operation grows as the input grows. "Cost" is usually time (number of steps) or space (memory). O(n) means "the work grows in proportion to the input size". O(1) means "the work does not depend on the input size". O(n²) means "double the input, quadruple the work".
11.10: Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level: first everything one step from the start, then everything two steps away, and so on. It uses a queue (first in, first out) and a visited set.
11.11: Depth-first search explores a graph by going as deep as it can along one path before backing up and trying the next. It uses a stack (the call stack when written recursively, or an explicit array) and a visited set.
11.12: A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges. Edges can be directed (A follows B) or undirected (A and B are friends), weighted (this road takes 4 minutes) or unweighted.
11.13: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the lowest-cost path from one start node to every other node in a graph whose edge weights are non-negative. It repeatedly takes the closest not-yet-finalized node, finalizes its distance, and relaxes its neighbors (updates their tentative distances if going through the current node is cheaper).
11.14: A topological order of a directed graph is a sequence of its nodes in which every edge points forward: if A must happen before B, A appears before B. It exists only if the graph has no cycles (a directed acyclic graph, DAG). Topological sorting is how you turn "these things depend on those things" into "do them in this order".
11.15: A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never going back to reconsider. Sort the options by some score, walk the list, take what fits. That is the whole strategy.
11.16: Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and remembering the answer. Two mechanics: memoization (top-down: write the recursive solution, cache results by input) and tabulation (bottom-up: fill a table from the smallest subproblems upward).
11.17: A rate limiter decides, for each incoming request, whether the caller has exceeded an allowed rate, and rejects it (usually with HTTP 429) if so.
11.2: Time complexity is Big O applied to running time: how many elementary steps an algorithm performs as a function of input size. The common classes, from cheapest to most expensive, are constant O(1), logarithmic O(log n), linear O(n), linearithmic O(n log n), quadratic O(n²), cubic O(n³) and exponential O(2ⁿ).
11.21: Worked example: search, from prefix tries to trigrams and pg_trgm

"Search" in a product backend usually means three different problems: prefix search (autocomplete: "iph" finds "iPhone 15"), substring or fuzzy search ("ipone" or "phone 15" finds "iPhone 15") and full-text search (ranked matching on words and stems across long text).
11.22: Worked example: dependency resolution with topological sort
Dependency resolution takes a set of things that declare what they need and produces an order (or a parallel schedule) in which every need is satisfied before it is used.
11.25: Everything from Part 10 — Computer Science Fundamentals: Data Structures and Part 11, consolidated. Time complexities are for the standard implementation; n is the number of elements.
11.5: Sorting arranges items in order by a key. Every "latest orders", "top sellers", "cheapest first" and every paginated list depends on a sort somewhere: in the database, in the application, or (best of all) in an index that was sorted when it was built.
11.6: Binary search finds a value in a sorted collection by repeatedly halving the search range. Look at the middle element; if it is what you want, stop; if it is smaller than the target, the target must be in the right half; otherwise, the left half.
11.7: The two-pointer technique walks through one or two sorted sequences with two indices that only ever move forward. Because neither pointer goes back, the total work is the sum of the lengths: O(n + m).
11.8: A sliding window is a fixed-size range that moves over a sequence, one step at a time, while you maintain some summary of what is inside it: a count, a sum, a maximum, an average.
11.9: Recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller piece of the problem until it reaches a piece small enough to answer directly (the base case).

12.4: Level 1 problems need one idea and usually one loop. They exist to make the method automatic and to practise the boring parts that cost points later: edge cases, off-by-one errors and clean tests. Aim to finish each within ten to fifteen minutes, tests included.
12.4.1: Pattern: hashing · Level 1 A payments API receives requests, each with an idempotency key, in arrival order. Return the first key whose second arrival happens earliest (that request is the first duplicate the server must reject), or null if there are no duplicates.
12.4.2: Pattern: counting · Level 1 Each log line has the form timestamp LEVEL CODE message.... Return the most frequent CODE among lines whose level is ERROR. If two codes tie, return the alphabetically smaller one. If there are no error lines, return null.
12.4.3: Pattern: stack · Level 1 A migration runner writes BEGIN name when a step starts and END name when it finishes. Steps can be nested (a step may start sub-steps). The log is valid if every END closes the most recently opened step that is still open, with the same name, and nothing is left open at the end.
12.4.4: Pattern: two pointers · Level 1 Two replicas each export the timestamps (integers, milliseconds) of events they saw, sorted ascending. The same event can appear in both, and a replica can list the same timestamp twice. Return one ascending list with every distinct timestamp exactly once. Do it in a single pass over both lists.
12.4.5: Pattern: prefix sums · Level 1 You have the revenue in cents for each of n days (n up to 10⁵; refunds can make a day negative). A finance dashboard sends up to 10⁵ queries [from, to] (0-based, inclusive) and wants the total for each range. Answer all queries faster than O(n) each.
12.4.6: Pattern: strings, two pointers · Level 1 Release versions look like 1.10.0 or 2.0. Write compareVersions(a, b) that returns -1 if a is older, 1 if a is newer and 0 if they are the same release. Missing parts count as 0 (2.0 equals 2.0.0), and leading zeros do not matter (1.01 equals 1.1). Pre-release tags are out of scope.
12.5: Level 2 is where the named patterns appear: complements in a hash map, fixed and variable sliding windows, sorting intervals, binary search, canonical keys, BFS and DFS. Each one is the simplest clean instance of its pattern.
12.5.1: Two orders that use up a gift card

Pattern: hashing (complements) · Level 2 A customer has a gift card with balance B cents and a list of past orders (id and amount). Support wants two different orders whose amounts add up to exactly B, to suggest a refund-to-card.
12.5.2: Pattern: fixed sliding window · Level 2 Given the number of requests in each minute of a day and a window size k, return the largest total over any k consecutive minutes, to size autoscaling. Return null if there are fewer than k minutes. n is up to 10⁶ and k can be large.
12.5.3: Shortest burst over an error budget

Pattern: variable sliding window · Level 2 Given the number of errors in each minute (all values are zero or positive) and a budget B, return the length of the shortest run of consecutive minutes whose total errors reach at least B. This is how quickly an incident can burn the budget. Return 0 if no run reaches it.
12.5.4: Pattern: sorting, intervals · Level 2 Several teams have booked maintenance windows as [start, end) minute ranges, in no particular order. Merge them into the smallest list of non-overlapping windows for the status page. Windows that overlap or touch ([10, 20) and [20, 30)) merge. Do not modify the input.
12.5.5: Pattern: binary search · Level 2 Builds are numbered 1 to n (n up to 10⁹ over the life of a monorepo). A test started failing at some build and has failed in every build since. You have isBroken(build), which takes minutes to run, so call it as few times as possible. Return the first broken build, or -1 if none is broken.
12.5.6: Pattern: hashing with a canonical key · Level 2 Marketing wants groups of customers whose carts contain exactly the same products in the same total quantities. Line order does not matter, and a product split across two lines counts as one (A x1, A x1 equals A x2).
12.5.7: Shortest path for a warehouse robot

Pattern: BFS on a grid · Level 2 A warehouse floor is a grid of strings: . is free floor, # is a shelf, S is the robot and P marks one or more packing stations. The robot moves one cell up, down, left or right per step. Return the fewest steps to reach any packing station, or -1 if none is reachable.
12.5.8: Pattern: DFS, connected components · Level 2 There are n servers numbered 0 to n - 1 and a list of network links, each joining two servers in both directions. A cluster is a group of servers that can all reach each other through links. Return the number of clusters and the size of the largest. n is up to 10⁵, links up to 2 × 10⁵.
12.6: Level 3 is the core of most interviews. Each problem combines two ideas: counting plus a heap, sorting plus a sweep, binary search plus a greedy check, prefix sums plus a hash map, a graph plus a queue. If you can solve these within 30 to 40 minutes while explaining your reasoning, you are ready for most backend coding rounds.
12.6.1: Pattern: heap, top-k · Level 3 You receive a stream of failed requests, each tagged with its endpoint ("POST /orders"). Return the k endpoints with the most failures, most failures first; break ties by endpoint name, alphabetically. There can be 10⁶ failures across 10⁵ endpoints, and k is small (say 10).
12.6.2: Free slots in a technician's day

Pattern: sorting, intervals · Level 3 A repair technician works from dayStart to dayEnd (minutes from midnight). Bookings are [start, end) ranges, unsorted, and may overlap each other or extend outside working hours.
12.6.3: Pattern: binary search on the answer · Level 3 A reporting system must run a list of export jobs in order. Job i processes rows[i] rows and cannot be split across nights. Each night the database can process at most C rows. Find the smallest C that finishes every job within D nights.
12.6.4: Day ranges with a given net balance

Pattern: prefix sums with hashing · Level 3 A wallet's daily net change is a list of integers (deposits positive, refunds and spending negative). Count how many runs of consecutive days have a net change of exactly k. n is up to 10⁵.
12.6.5: Pattern: topological sort · Level 3 A platform deploys services in waves: all services in a wave go out in parallel, and a service may only be in a wave after every service it depends on has gone out in an earlier wave.
12.6.6: Pattern: shortest path (Dijkstra) · Level 3 Traffic between regions travels over directed links, each with a measured latency in milliseconds (all non-negative). Given the links, a source region and a target region, return the lowest total latency and the route, or null if the target is unreachable.
12.6.7: Coupon combinations for an exact total

Pattern: backtracking · Level 3 A support agent can compensate a customer with promotional coupons. Given the available coupon values (there may be several coupons with the same value; each coupon can be used once) and a target amount, list every distinct combination of values that adds up exactly to the target.
12.6.8: Pattern: 1-D dynamic programming · Level 3 A warehouse ships items in boxes of a few fixed capacities (for example 1, 4 and 5 items), and every box must be full. Given the capacities and an order of n items (n up to 10⁴), return the fewest boxes, or -1 if no combination fits exactly.
12.6.9: Pattern: monotonic deque · Level 3 Given the response times of the last n requests (n up to 10⁶) and a window size k, return the slowest response time in every window of k consecutive requests, for a latency dashboard. There are n - k + 1 windows.
12.7.1: Pattern: 2-D dynamic programming · Level 4 Two services wrote audit logs for the same order, as lists of event names. Find the longest sequence of events that appears in both logs in the same order (not necessarily adjacent): the events they agree on. The rest is the diff. Each log has up to 2,000 events.
12.7.2: Pattern: trie · Level 4 Build an autocomplete index for product names. add(name, popularity) adds a product or updates its popularity. suggest(prefix) returns up to three product names that start with the prefix (ignoring case), most popular first, ties broken alphabetically.
12.7.3: The link that created a loop

Pattern: union-find · Level 4 Network links between n switches are added one at a time. A loop (a cycle) causes broadcast storms, so the provisioning tool must report the first link whose two ends were already connected through earlier links. Return that link, or null. Up to 10⁵ switches and links.
12.7.4: Most maintenance jobs in one night

Pattern: greedy · Level 4 Teams request maintenance jobs on a shared database, each as [start, end) minutes within the maintenance night. Jobs cannot overlap. Choose the largest possible number of jobs and return their ids. Explain why your choice is optimal. Up to 10⁵ requests.
12.7.5: Cheapest courier route with few hand-offs

Pattern: graph, bounded relaxation · Level 4 A parcel must travel from hub src to hub dst. Courier legs are directed, each with a cost in cents. Every intermediate hub is a hand-off, and each hand-off risks loss, so the route may use at most k hand-offs (at most k + 1 legs). Return the cheapest cost, or -1.
12.7.6: Longest rising run of order values

Pattern: dynamic programming with binary search · Level 4 For a loyalty analysis, find the length of the longest sequence of a customer's orders (in date order, not necessarily consecutive) whose values strictly increase. A customer can have up to 10⁵ orders.
12.7.7: Smallest log window with every required code

Pattern: variable sliding window with counts · Level 4 During an incident you want the shortest stretch of consecutive log entries that contains every code on a checklist, with multiplicity (if the checklist has E_DB twice, the window needs two E_DB entries).

13.1: A process is a running program. When you type node dist/main.js, the kernel creates a process: it gets a process id (PID), its own private virtual address space (memory that no other process can see), its own table of open file descriptors (files, sockets, pipes), its own environment variables, its own signal handlers, and at least one thread of execution.
13.10: A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) is a lock with one holder. Whoever holds it may run the protected code (the critical section); everyone else waits until it is released. It is the simplest tool for turning a multi-step sequence into something that behaves as if it were one step.
13.12: An atomic operation is one that cannot be observed half-done and cannot interleave with another operation on the same target. Either it happened entirely or not at all, and no one saw the middle.
13.13: Garbage collection (GC) is automatic reclamation of memory that a program can no longer reach. You allocate objects freely; a collector periodically finds which objects are still reachable from the program's roots (the call stack, global variables, closures currently in scope, native handles such as open sockets and timers) and frees everything else.
13.15: The call stack is the per-thread stack region from 13.3 as seen from JavaScript: a last-in-first-out list of frames, one per function call in progress. Calling a function pushes a frame holding its arguments, local variables and the return address; returning pops it. The stack trace you see on an error is a walk down this list.
13.16: The event loop is the program that runs your program. It is a loop inside libuv, on the main thread, that repeatedly asks the kernel "what is ready?" and runs the JavaScript callbacks for whatever is: an incoming HTTP request, a PostgreSQL response, a timer that has expired, a file read that finished.
13.17: A macrotask (or just "task") is one callback from one of the loop's phases: a timer firing, an I/O completion, a setImmediate, a close event.
13.18: libuv is the C library that gives Node.js its asynchronous behaviour. V8 (3.14) runs JavaScript; libuv does everything else: it owns the event loop (13.16), it talks to the kernel's readiness notification mechanism (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows), it manages timers, TCP and UDP sockets, pipes, signals, child processes, DNS, and it owns a small pool of real operating-system threads for the work …
13.19: Async I/O: epoll, kqueue and IOCP

For sockets, Node does not use threads at all. It asks the kernel a single question — "which of these 10,000 file descriptors can I read from or write to right now?" — and the kernel answers in one syscall.
13.2: CPU scheduling is how the kernel decides which runnable thread gets which CPU core, and for how long. A core can run exactly one thread at a time. If there are more runnable threads than cores, the scheduler gives each a time slice (typically a few milliseconds), then switches.
13.20: A worker thread is a second JavaScript execution context inside the same process: its own V8 isolate, its own heap, its own event loop, its own call stack — running on a real operating-system thread, scheduled independently by the kernel on a different core.
13.21: A child process is a separate operating-system process that your Node process starts and controls. It has its own PID, its own memory, its own file descriptors, and its own lifetime. Node gives you four ways to create one, and the differences between them are the source of a surprising number of production incidents.
13.22: The cluster module forks N copies of your Node process — one per CPU core, typically — and lets them share a single listening port. Incoming connections are distributed across the workers, so a machine with 8 cores runs 8 event loops instead of 1.
13.23: A stream is an interface for moving data a piece at a time instead of all at once. Instead of "read the whole 4 GB file into a Buffer, then write it", you read 64 KB, write 64 KB, and repeat — so peak memory is one chunk, not one file.
13.24: Backpressure is the feedback signal that tells a fast producer to slow down because a slow consumer cannot keep up. Without it, the difference between production rate and consumption rate accumulates somewhere — and in Node, "somewhere" is always the heap.
13.25: A memory leak in a garbage-collected runtime is not memory the collector forgot. V8's collector is correct: it frees everything unreachable.

14.4: TCP and UDP: the transport layer

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) gives two processes a reliable, ordered byte stream over an unreliable network. You write bytes in one end; they come out the other end in the same order, with nothing missing and nothing duplicated, or the connection reports an error. TCP has no idea what a "message" or an "HTTP request" is.

34.2: A timeout is a decision, made in advance, about how long you are willing to wait for something before you give up and do something else. It is the single most important reliability control you have, because it is the only thing that converts an unbounded wait into a bounded one.
34.3: A retry is a second attempt at an operation that failed, on the theory that the failure was transient: a dropped packet, a pod that was mid-restart, a brief lock wait, a rate-limit window. 34.4: Backoff is the wait between retry attempts. Exponential backoff makes each wait roughly double the previous one (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms), so a struggling dependency gets progressively more breathing room.
34.5: A circuit breaker is a stateful wrapper around calls to one dependency. It watches the recent failure rate. While the dependency is healthy the breaker is closed and calls pass through. 34.6: A bulkhead is an isolation boundary that limits how many resources one workload or one dependency can consume, so that its failure cannot take resources from the others. 34.7: Rate limiting caps how many operations a caller may perform in a time window. It appears in two directions. Inbound rate limiting protects you from clients (abusive, buggy, or simply enthusiastic).
34.8: Load shedding is deliberately rejecting some requests when the system is overloaded, so that the requests you do accept complete within their deadline. It is rate limiting driven by your own health rather than by a caller's quota.
34.9: Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow consumer tells a fast producer to slow down. Load shedding rejects work at the edge; backpressure propagates the "I'm full" signal upstream so that producers stop generating work faster than it can be handled.

35.4: A deadlock is a cycle of waiting. Transaction A holds a lock that transaction B wants, and B holds a lock that A wants. Neither can proceed, and neither will ever give up voluntarily. 88.1: Why writing is the architect's primary tool
Writing is how an architect scales past the reach of their own hands and their own voice. A conversation persuades the people in the room, once, and then decays.
88.2: Document types and when to use each

There is not one architect's document; there is a small family of them, and each has a job. Using the wrong one is like using a screwdriver as a chisel — it sort of works, and it ruins both the tool and the work. A one-pager is for getting a quick yes on a direction. An RFC is for getting many teams to agree on a change.
88.3: The anatomy of a strong design doc
A design doc has a skeleton, and the skeleton is not decoration. Each section exists to answer a question a serious reviewer will ask, in the order they ask it.
88.4: Writing alternatives honestly, and running the RFC process

Two skills live together here because they are the heart of getting a design agreed. The first is writing the alternatives you rejected honestly, so reviewers trust that you actually considered them rather than building a lineup of strawmen to make your favourite look good.
88.5: Running design reviews, and diagrams that earn their place
Two more skills that make documents work. The first is running a design review well — both as the author presenting your work and as a reviewer critiquing someone else's.

We have referred to this RFC throughout the Part. Here it is in full, as a single artifact you can read end to end and use as a template. 88.7: ADR chains, keeping docs alive, and the anti-patterns

Three final threads that separate people who write documents from people whose documents still matter years later. The first is the ADR chain: how a sequence of decision records tells the story of a choice made, lived with, and eventually replaced — because decisions have a life, and the record should show it.
88.8: Reusable templates and building the writing habit

Everything in this Part becomes real only if you can produce it on a normal Tuesday without heroics. Two things make that possible. The first is a small set of reusable templates — skeletons you copy and fill, so you are never staring at a blank page and never forgetting a section under deadline pressure.
88.9: The post-incident review as a document, and writing at scale

Two topics that extend the Part's craft. The post-incident review (PIR) is a document type with its own discipline: a blameless account of what broke, a precise timeline, the real root cause, and tracked actions — written so the organisation learns rather than assigns blame.
89.1: Strategy versus vision versus roadmap versus plan

Four words get used interchangeably and mean four different things, and conflating them is the root of most bad "strategy" documents. A strategy is a way of overcoming a specific challenge: a diagnosis of the situation, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and a set of coherent actions.
89.3: Building a multi-quarter roadmap: sequencing, dependencies and capacity

A roadmap turns a strategy into a sequence of initiatives over time. The craft is not drawing the Gantt chart; it is the sequencing — deciding what comes before what, so that dependencies are respected, risk is front-loaded, early wins build momentum, and the plan fits the capacity you actually have rather than the capacity you wish you had.
89.4: Managing technical debt as a portfolio
Technical debt is usually treated as a guilty backlog — an undifferentiated pile of "stuff we should clean up someday" that always loses to features.
89.5: New technology arrives constantly, and someone on your team always wants to adopt the latest thing. Evaluating technology well means having a repeatable process: explicit evaluation criteria, a proof of concept designed to answer a real question, a total-cost-of-ownership calculation that includes the costs people forget, an honest look at the exit cost (how hard is it to leave), and a staged adoption model so you …

Three connected skills that round out strategy. Build vs buy at company scale extends the Part 68.19 decision table into the territory that only matters at scale: vendor risk, lock-in, contract terms, and what happens when a vendor is acquired or raises prices.
89.8: Communicating, measuring, and sustaining a strategy

A strategy that is written but not communicated, measured, or sustained is a document, not a direction. Three disciplines turn a strategy kernel into a living force in the organisation: communicating it so people actually internalise it (repetition until bored, embedding it in decisions), measuring it so you know whether it is working and can adjust (leading indicators, checkpoints, falsifiable signals), and …
89.9: Strategy anti-patterns and the strategy review
Two final tools. The strategy anti-patterns are the recurring ways technical strategy goes wrong, gathered into one catalogue so you can recognise and avoid them.
9.1: The single most useful idea in TypeScript is this: a type is a set of values. boolean is the set {true, false}. The literal type 'paid' is the set containing exactly one string. string is the infinite set of all strings. A union 'pending' | 'paid' is the union of two sets.
9.1.2: TypeScript is structurally typed: a value fits a type if it has the right shape, regardless of what it was called or which class created it. Java and C# are mostly nominally typed: a value fits only if it was declared as that type or a subtype. In TypeScript, names are labels for shapes, not identities.
9.10: Branded types for IDs and money

A branded type (also called a nominal or opaque type) is a primitive with an invisible tag attached at the type level, so that two values with the same runtime shape become incompatible types: an OrderId cannot be passed where a CustomerId is expected, though both are strings at runtime.
9.12: Type-safe API contracts end to end

TypeScript types disappear at runtime (1.2.1), so they cannot check a request body. A validator checks it at runtime. The engineering problem is keeping the two in step: the type that the service code trusts must describe exactly what the validator lets through.
9.13: Typing NestJS: repositories, configuration and events

NestJS gives you dependency injection, decorators and a module system; it does not make your configuration, repositories or in-process events type-safe by itself. Three small patterns close the most common leaks: a narrow generic repository, typed configuration, and a typed event facade.
9.14: Declaration files and augmenting third-party types

A declaration file (.d.ts) contains only types: no runtime code. It describes JavaScript that exists elsewhere. Packages ship them (the types field in package.json), the community publishes them for untyped packages as @types/* (DefinitelyTyped), and tsc emits them for your own libraries with declaration: true. declare module lets you describe a module that has no types, and module augmentation lets you add to a type …
9.16: Type checking costs CPU and memory. In a large monorepo, a full tsc can take minutes and the editor can lag seconds behind your typing. Most of that time usually comes from a few expensive types or configuration mistakes, not from the size of the code itself.
9.2: Narrowing is how TypeScript moves a value down the set diagram: from a wide type such as string | null or unknown to a narrower one, based on a check the code has done.
9.2.2: Part 1 (1.7.2) introduced the discriminated union and the never check. In depth, the rule is: a union of object types narrows on a discriminant, a property whose type is a different literal in each member.
9.3: Part 1 (1.7.3) showed a generic as a type with a blank to fill in, and a constraint as T extends { id: string }. In depth, a generic function is a relationship between types: "whatever comes in, this is what goes out".
9.3.3: Variance answers: if a PaidOrder is a kind of Order, is a "box of PaidOrder" a kind of "box of Order"? It depends on what the box does with its contents.
9.4: Three operators let you derive a type instead of writing it again: Derived types cannot drift from their source. When the source changes, everything derived from it changes with it.
9.5: A conditional type chooses between two types based on a test: T extends U ? X : Y, read "if T is assignable to U, then X, else Y". The infer keyword, used inside the test, captures a part of T into a new type variable, like a regular-expression capture group for types.
9.6: A mapped type builds a new object type by walking over a set of keys and computing a property for each: { [K in Keys]: SomeTypeUsing }. It is a for loop over keys, run by the compiler. Key remapping (as) lets the loop rename keys or drop them.
9.8: The built-in utility types and writing your own
TypeScript ships a set of generic utility types built from the mechanisms above. Knowing them saves writing them, and makes your types readable to anyone who knows TypeScript.
90.1: Why governance exists, and why heavy governance fails

Governance exists to produce consistency and quality across many teams that would otherwise each make their own choices, leading to a system nobody can operate. Without any governance, forty teams produce forty error formats, forty logging conventions, forty ways to paginate, and an operational nightmare.
90.2: A paved road (also called a golden path) is the well-supported, opinionated, default way to do a common thing — create a service, add a queue consumer, expose an API — where all the hard decisions have been made for you and all the standard pieces come pre-wired.
90.3: Standards are the shared conventions that let services across an org interoperate and be operated together: a standard API shape, a standard event schema format, a standard error format, standard logging and metrics conventions, standard naming.
90.4: Architecture review boards and their lightweight alternatives

An architecture review board (ARB) is a group of senior engineers who review and approve architectural decisions. They can be genuinely valuable — a place to catch cross-cutting mistakes and share hard-won judgement — or they can become the bottleneck and ivory tower from 90.1.
90.5: An architecture fitness function is an automated test that checks whether the system still has the architectural properties you want: that layers are respected, that dependency rules hold, that latency stays within budget, that bundle sizes do not balloon.
90.6: Dependency policy, shared libraries, waivers and measuring compliance

Four governance topics that come up once you have many services. Dependency and version policy is how you handle the constant churn of upgrades across dozens of services — upgrade cadence, support windows, end-of-life handling.
90.8: Event schema governance and the schema registry

Of all the standards an organisation needs, event schemas are among the most important and most often neglected. When services communicate through events (Part 31), every event has a shape, and if those shapes are inconsistent or change incompatibly, consumers break.
91.1: Why large migrations fail: the 80% done forever problem

Large migrations rarely fail by exploding. They fail by stalling — getting to roughly 80% complete and staying there indefinitely. The first 80% is the exciting, high-value, straightforward part: migrate the main services, the common cases, the cooperative teams.
91.2: Running a migration as a program

A large migration is not a project; it is a program — a long-running, multi-team effort that needs its own scoping, milestones, owners, tracking, and communication cadence, run with the same discipline as a product launch.
91.3: There is no single way to do a migration; there is a family of strategies, each with a different risk profile, and choosing the right one for your situation is a principal-level decision.
91.4: Monolith decomposition: seams, the first service, and data ownership

Breaking a monolith into services is the most common large migration, and the hardest part is not the code — it is the data. Decomposition means finding the seams (the natural boundaries where the monolith can be split), extracting the first service (which is disproportionately hard because you are building all the platform scaffolding for the first time), splitting data ownership (deciding which service owns which …
91.5: Data migrations at scale: dual writes, CDC, backfills, and reconciliation
Moving the data itself — billions of rows from an old store to a new one, while the system keeps running and the data keeps changing — is the hardest technical part of most migrations.
91.6: Deprecating, platform migrations, and risk management

Three topics that complete the migration toolkit. Deprecating and turning things off is the discipline of actually removing the old system — using usage telemetry to find the real callers, deprecation notices and brownouts to push them off, and specific tactics for the stubborn last 5%.

This section brings the whole Part together in one eighteen-month migration: moving an order system from a PHP monolith on MySQL to NestJS services on PostgreSQL.
92.1: Conway's Law and the inverse Conway maneuver

Conway's Law, stated by Melvin Conway in 1967, is: organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. In plain terms: the way your teams are divided and the way they talk to each other will be reflected in the way your software is divided and the way its parts talk to each other.
92.2: Team topologies: the four team types and interaction modes

Team Topologies, from the book of the same name by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, gives a vocabulary for designing teams deliberately. It says there are really only four fundamental team types you need — stream-aligned, platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem — and three ways teams should interact — collaboration, X-as-a-service, and facilitating.
92.3: Two linked ideas that determine whether teams can actually operate what they own. Cognitive load is the total amount of stuff a team has to hold in their heads to do their job — the systems they own, the domains they must understand, the tools they must operate.
92.4: Platform engineering and the internal developer platform

Platform engineering is the discipline of building an internal platform that makes the stream-aligned teams faster and more self-sufficient — treating that platform as a product, with the stream-aligned teams as its customers.
92.5: Developer experience (DevEx or DX) is how it feels, day to day, to build and ship software in your organisation — how long a change takes from idea to production, how long builds take, how often deploys fail, how much toil engineers endure, how satisfied they are.
92.6: When to reorganise, and the architect's role in the org

Two topics that close the org-design toolkit. The first is knowing when to split a team, merge services, or reorganise — treating a reorg not as a disruptive political event but as a deliberate architectural change, because (per Conway's Law) changing the org changes the software.
93.1: Influencing without authority is getting people who do not report to you to change what they do — adopt your standard, prioritise your project, stop doing a thing — through means other than command.
93.2: Stakeholder mapping and communicating with executives

Two skills that determine whether your influence reaches the people who matter. Stakeholder mapping is working out, for any initiative, who decides, who is affected, and who can block — so you spend your influence effort on the right people rather than broadcasting equally to everyone.
93.3: A business case is the quantified argument that an investment is worth making, in the terms a business uses to decide: return on investment (ROI), cost of delay, the value of reducing risk, and opportunity cost.
93.5: Saying no, presenting to mixed audiences, and running decision forums

Three skills that round out the communication toolkit. Saying no and negotiating scope is the discipline of declining or reshaping work so the team is not overloaded and thrashed — saying no with alternatives, negotiating which of scope/time/quality moves, and protecting the team from the constant churn of shifting priorities.
94.1: Three distinct ways of developing people that are often confused. Mentoring is sharing your experience and advice — "here is how I would approach this, here is what I learned". Coaching is helping someone find their own answer through questions, without giving it to them — "what options do you see, what would happen if...".
94.3: Onboarding programs that cut time to first meaningful change

Onboarding is how a new engineer goes from day one to being a productive, contributing member of the team. A good onboarding program is designed and measured, with a clear metric: time to first meaningful change — how long until a new hire ships something real to production.
94.4: Designing an interview loop for backend roles

An interview loop is the sequence of interviews a candidate goes through. Designing one well means deciding what signal each stage is meant to produce — coding ability, system design judgement, debugging skill, collaboration, backend depth — and ensuring each stage produces a distinct signal, so you are not running redundant stages that measure the same thing while leaving important signals untested.
94.5: Writing questions and rubrics, calibration, and avoiding bias

Good interviewing depends on good instruments and good process. Writing interview questions and rubrics means crafting questions that elicit the target signal and rubrics that define what a strong, mixed, and weak answer looks like, so evaluation is consistent rather than based on gut feeling.
94.6: Running a system design interview, and building a technical culture

Two final skills. Running a system design interview as the interviewer is a distinct craft from being the candidate: steering the conversation, probing for depth at the right moments, giving the candidate room to show their judgement, and scoring against a rubric — all while making it a good experience.
95.1: Multi-tenancy models: silo, pool, and bridge

A multi-tenancy model is how you divide tenants across your infrastructure. There are three main models. Silo gives each tenant their own isolated stack (separate database, sometimes separate everything). Pool shares one stack across all tenants, with data separated logically by a tenant_id.
95.2: Tenant isolation in PostgreSQL: row-level security

In the pool model, tenant isolation depends on every query touching only the current tenant's rows. Relying on application code to always add WHERE tenant_id = ... is dangerous, because one forgotten filter is a cross-tenant breach.
95.3: The tenant context is how your NestJS application knows, for every request, which tenant it is serving — and makes that known reliably to every layer (guards, services, repositories, the RLS session variable) without passing it manually through every function call.
95.4: Noisy neighbours: per-tenant rate limits, quotas, and fair queuing

In a pooled multi-tenant system, tenants share resources — CPU, database connections, queue capacity, API throughput. A noisy neighbour is a tenant whose heavy usage degrades the experience of other tenants sharing the same resources: one tenant running a huge batch job, or sending a flood of requests, can starve everyone else.
95.5: Per-tenant configuration, entitlements, plans, and billing hooks

Tenants are not identical: they are on different plans, have different features enabled, different limits, and different settings. Per-tenant configuration is how each tenant customises behaviour (settings, branding, preferences).
95.6: Enterprise B2B features and data residency

Enterprise customers demand features that consumer and small-business SaaS do not need, and lacking them blocks enterprise deals entirely. The core enterprise B2B features are: SSO (single sign-on via SAML or OIDC, so enterprise users log in with their corporate identity provider), SCIM (automated user provisioning and deprovisioning from the customer's identity system), customer-readable audit logs (so the …
95.7: Compliance-driven architecture, integration patterns, and tenant lifecycle

Three topics that complete the enterprise SaaS picture. Compliance-driven architecture is how regulations shape your system design: GDPR (right to erasure, data export/portability), PCI DSS (reducing the scope of systems that touch card data), SOC 2 (controls and auditability), and HIPAA (protected health information) each impose concrete architectural requirements.
95.8: Worked example: turning a single-tenant inventory product into a multi-tenant SaaS

This section brings the whole Part together: converting a single-tenant inventory management product into a multi-tenant SaaS. It is the canonical "make it multi-tenant" problem, and it exercises every concept in this Part — the tenancy model, RLS isolation, tenant context, noisy-neighbour control, entitlements, enterprise features, compliance, and lifecycle.
96.10: Running a security programme across teams
A security programme is how an organisation makes security happen continuously across all its teams, not only when the security team is in the room.
96.11: Security reviews and the architect's design checklist
A security design review examines a proposed system or significant change before it is built, against threats and principles, and produces decisions and actions.
96.13: Worked architecture: security for a multi-tenant SaaS

Every request carries a session issued after authentication (local MFA, or the tenant's IdP via SSO); the gateway resolves the tenant from the session, never from a header the client controls, and passes a signed internal token with user, tenant and roles to services.
96.4: Zero trust is a security model in which no request is trusted because of where it comes from on the network. Every access, by a person or a workload, is authenticated, authorised against policy and encrypted, every time, based on identity and context (device health, location, time, sensitivity of the resource) rather than on being "inside" the corporate network or VPC.
96.5: Identity architecture is the design of every kind of identity in the organisation, human and machine, and how each is created, authenticated, authorised, reviewed and removed: employees and contractors through a central identity provider (IdP) with SSO; customers through the product's own identity system or their enterprise IdP; service accounts and workloads through platform-issued, short-lived credentials; and the …
96.6: Even in a zero-trust design, the network and the cloud account structure remain powerful controls for blast radius and data exfiltration. Segmentation divides the environment so a compromise in one area cannot reach others; private connectivity keeps traffic to cloud services and partners off the public internet; egress control decides what may leave; and a landing zone is the pre-built, governed multi-account cloud …
96.7: Data security architecture decides how data is protected according to its sensitivity across its whole life: classification (what kind of data it is), encryption in transit, at rest and in use, tokenisation (replacing sensitive values with substitutes), key ownership (who controls the keys, including customers), and residency (where it may live).
96.8: Part 44.28 covered supply-chain hygiene for a service: committed lockfiles, npm ci --ignore-scripts, audits, a registry proxy, image scanning and an SBOM per build.
96.9: Prevention fails eventually. Detection and response architecture decides what evidence the organisation collects (logging strategy), where it is analysed (SIEM and detection pipelines), how alerts are made trustworthy (alert quality), and how people respond (incident response roles, runbooks and exercises).
97.1: How staff, principal and architect loops differ from senior loops

A staff-plus loop is a set of interviews designed to find evidence of leverage: decisions, designs, standards and people that made several teams better over one to five years (Part 63 — Junior to Principal: What Is Expected at Each Level, section 63.1).

This round, sometimes split into a behavioural round and a conversation with a senior leader, tests how you get things done through people you do not manage, how you disagree and then commit, how you make a case in money terms, and how you explain trade-offs to executives briefly.

At staff and principal level, the company is choosing you, and you are choosing the problems, the sponsor and the organisation you will spend the next several years on.
